lesson.title: Magnitude and Angle: Why Polar Form Makes Multiplication Painless
lesson.summary: Polar form writes a complex number as a magnitude and an angle rather than real and imaginary parts, turning the multiplication and division inside Ohm's law into simple arithmetic on those two numbers.
lesson.body:
Polar form writes a complex number as z = r angle theta, shorthand for r(cos theta + j sin theta), where r is the magnitude, the distance from the origin, and theta is the angle measured counterclockwise from the positive real axis. It is the same complex number as its rectangular form a + jb, just described using distance and direction instead of horizontal and vertical components, and converting between the two uses the standard right triangle relationships r = sqrt(a^2 + b^2) and theta = arctan(b/a).

Take the series impedance from the previous chapter, Z = 5 + j3 ohms. Its magnitude is r = sqrt(5^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(34) = 5.831 ohms, and its angle is theta = arctan(3/5) = arctan(0.6) = 30.96 degrees. In polar form, that same impedance is written Z = 5.831 angle 30.96 degrees ohms. Both forms describe the identical physical impedance, one location in the complex plane, just expressed with different coordinates.

The payoff for switching to polar form shows up the moment you need to multiply or divide. To multiply two complex numbers in polar form, multiply their magnitudes and add their angles: (r1 angle theta1)(r2 angle theta2) = r1 r2 angle (theta1 + theta2). To divide, divide the magnitudes and subtract the angles. That is dramatically simpler than the full rectangular multiplication rule from the last chapter, and it matters directly because Ohm's law for phasors, V = I times Z, is exactly this kind of multiplication.

Suppose a phasor current I = 2 angle (-15 degrees) A flows through an impedance Z = 10 angle 30 degrees ohms. Ohm's law gives the phasor voltage V = I times Z. Multiply the magnitudes: 2 times 10 = 20. Add the angles: -15 degrees + 30 degrees = 15 degrees. So V = 20 angle 15 degrees V. Doing that same multiplication in rectangular form would have required converting both numbers to a + jb first, then applying the full (ac - bd) + j(ad + bc) rule, several extra steps for an answer that polar form reaches in one line.

Angles in polar form are usually kept within the range -180 degrees to +180 degrees, or equivalently -pi to +pi radians, by adding or subtracting 360 degrees whenever a calculation like the addition rule above pushes the result outside that window. Nothing about the underlying number changes when this is done, since 380 degrees and 20 degrees describe exactly the same direction in the complex plane, only the labeling convention is being kept tidy.

This is why AC circuit analysis constantly shuttles between the two forms covered in these two chapters: rectangular form for any addition or subtraction, such as combining series impedances or parallel admittances, and polar form for any multiplication or division, such as applying Ohm's law or computing power. Neither form is more correct than the other, since both describe the same complex numbers built on the same underlying idea of a real and an imaginary axis, but picking the right one for the operation at hand is what keeps AC calculations from turning into unnecessary algebra.
